While working on the Advent of Code Challenge for this year, I planned to solve the challenges in Python and the Rust Programming Language, and after solving the first 2 days in Python, I decided to solve those in Rust too, it didn’t take long before I realized how difficult I found it working with Rust programs without the benefits of a Language server like Rust Analyzer.

The Problem

Rust Analyzer is built around Cargo. When you run:

cargo new my_project

Cargo quietly generates the metadata Rust Analyzer relies on to understand your code: crate boundaries, dependencies, edition, and access to the standard library.

But when you’re working with:

  • a single .rs file
  • a mixed-language repository
  • small, disposable programs (like Advent of Code)

You lose all of that context. Rust Analyzer has nothing to latch onto, and the editor experience degrades sharply.

Unlike Python, where tooling scales gracefully from one file to one thousand, Rust’s tooling assumes Cargo by default.

Motivation

Conventionally, when you start a new Rust project with cargo new <project_name>, cargo generates some configuration about your project which your Rust analyzer picks and uses to provide useful autocompletion features, go to definition support, and inline type hinting.

But when working with simpler setups like a single Rust file, you lose out on the benefits that come with the Rust analyzer and the Cargo project configuration. Unlike Programming languages like Python, which can work straightforwardly as single files and as complex project structures.
Of course, with the benefits of the autocompletion and the rest, you can still very well write and compile single file rust programs.

After stumbling into a bug while implementing a solution for the challenges in Advent of Code day 2 in Rust, and I realized how much harder it was to walkthrough the types in my program visually and get support for autocompletion, method names and signatures, I decided to do an internet search on how to configure Rust Analyzer to work for single file rust Project without Cargo.

While searching, I came across many such advice;

People kept generally hinting at using cargo, but, like in my case, it was not reasonable to set up a cargo project for every single day’s challenge, and it was a multi-language environment, and not a Rust-specific project.

In my case:

  • Each Advent of Code solution was a standalone program
  • The repository contained multiple languages
  • Creating and maintaining a Cargo project per day felt like overkill

I didn’t want a build system.
I wanted my editor to understand Rust.

Solution

Rust Analyzer has support for non-cargo based project, just like the use case I wished to use it for above, but to give Rust Analyzer details on your setup and directory to find standard Rust libraries, you have to provide these details in a rust-project.json file in the root directory containing the single Rust files you wish to work on without Cargo. See details here.

With a small amount of explicit configuration, you can give Rust Analyzer everything it needs:

  • where Rust is installed
  • which files are crates
  • which edition to use

No Cargo required.

# rust-project.json

{
  "sysroot": "/Users/Apple/.rustup/toolchains/stable-aarch64-apple-darwin",
  "crates": [
    {
      "display_name": "core",
      "root_module": "/Users/Apple/.rustup/toolchains/stable-aarch64-apple-darwin/lib/rustlib/src/rust/library/core/src/lib.rs",
      "edition": "2024",
      "deps": [],
      "cfg": [
        "target_arch=\"aarch64\"",
        "target_os=\"macos\"",
        "unix"
      ],
      "env": {},
      "is_proc_macro": false
    },
    {
      "display_name": "alloc",
      "root_module": "/Users/Apple/.rustup/toolchains/stable-aarch64-apple-darwin/lib/rustlib/src/rust/library/alloc/src/lib.rs",
      "edition": "2024",
      "deps": [
        { "crate": 0, "name": "core" }
      ],
      "cfg": [
        "target_arch=\"aarch64\"",
        "target_os=\"macos\"",
        "unix"
      ],
      "env": {},
      "is_proc_macro": false
    },
    {
      "display_name": "std",
      "root_module": "/Users/Apple/.rustup/toolchains/stable-aarch64-apple-darwin/lib/rustlib/src/rust/library/std/src/lib.rs",
      "edition": "2024",
      "deps": [
        { "crate": 0, "name": "core" },
        { "crate": 1, "name": "alloc" }
      ],
      "cfg": [
        "target_arch=\"aarch64\"",
        "target_os=\"macos\"",
        "unix"
      ],
      "env": {},
      "is_proc_macro": false
    },
    {
      "display_name": "day_4",
      "root_module": "/Users/Apple/Documents/advent-of-codes/2025/day_4.rs",
      "edition": "2024",
      "deps": [{ "crate": 2, "name": "std" }],
      "cfg": [
        "target_arch=\"aarch64\"",
        "target_os=\"macos\"",
        "unix"
      ],
      "env": {},
      "is_proc_macro": false
    },
    {
      "display_name": "day_5",
      "root_module": "/Users/Apple/Documents/advent-of-codes/2025/day_5.rs",
      "edition": "2024",
      "deps": [{ "crate": 2, "name": "std" }],
      "cfg": [
        "target_arch=\"aarch64\"",
        "target_os=\"macos\"",
        "unix"
      ],
      "env": {},
      "is_proc_macro": false
    }
  ]
}

Explanation:

  • sysroot: Tells Rust Analyzer where your Rust toolchain lives—the standard library, core, alloc, and compiler support crates.
    You can get this value by entering the following command
rustc --print sysroot
  • crates: An array describing each logical Rust crate in the workspace.
    For simple setups, this often maps** one-to-one with a single .rs file**, but it can also represent larger module trees.
    Take note to pass the Absolute path of the root_module attribute

Notice that the first 3 crates are standard crates that Rust Analyzer needs to annotate builtin traits properly, ensure that you own defined crates (single Rust files) that depend on those traits to gain the complete type annotation benefits.

After creating and saving this file to your working directory, you should reload your editor workspace to get all the great benefits of Rust Analyzer working on your single-file Rust Programs (non-Cargo projects)

Conclusion

Rust doesn’t stop you from writing small, single-file programs, but without proper tooling, it certainly makes you feel the absence. Rust Analyzer, by default, expects Cargo to be the narrator of your project’s story, and when Cargo is missing, the editor is left guessing in the dark.

The good news is that this limitation is not a dead end. By explicitly describing your setup using a rust-project.json file, you can restore nearly all the ergonomics you’d expect from a full Cargo-based project: autocomplete, type hints, navigation, and a clearer understanding of your code’s structure.

For lightweight experiments, coding challenges, or mixed-language repositories, this approach strikes a practical balance. You keep the simplicity of single-file Rust while reclaiming the insight and confidence that come from a well-informed editor.

Sometimes, the compiler already knows enough. You just need to teach your tools to listen.

entry.title: Starting Today, I'm Going Deeper into Game Development with Rust
entry.content:
TL;DR
I am documenting my first entry in a series of articles that will come after this one on the topic of game development. I also intend to use this as a Medium to create the sort of learning material I would have appreciated a lot, following through on my game development hobby.

Motivation

Game development has been one of my most desired areas in the software technology sphere, one I have adored with great passion and interest. The ability to create immersive worlds and universes that defined their own rules and had a significant gravitational impact on their fanbase. And most times, it wasn’t just the universes that made people love games, it was the storytelling, the narrative it creates, the characterization, and a lot more in between. This is the part I want to understand and eventually master.

Background

My Journey of tinkering and building software has followed the web development route. From my days of creating web pages with HTML, CSS, and Bootstrap, through my experience building dynamic web pages with Django, I am currently focused on building backend infrastructures for RESTful APIs.

But moving forward, I want to dedicate my free time to researching and creating games, and I want to follow a very academic-inclined methodology, going on deep dives into game development concepts and standards.

“Preparing to do the thing isn’t doing the thing.

Scheduling time to do the thing isn’t doing the thing.

Making a to-do list for the thing isn’t doing the thing.

… Go and do the thing.”—Chris Williamson

So this is me: doing the thing.

Beginning the Work Proper

Game development involves developing the interface and logic of a game. Now there are some toolings out there that make it easy by offering visual tools to customize the different components of your game, but I intend to follow the old way, learning and building every part of my game piece by piece, as was the way of my father before me.

For one, this is a sure way to gain mastery in this topic, but it also ensures that my ability to create worlds is not limited to the tooling at hand, but to my skills with the crude tool (a Programming language). I am sure along my journey, I would have needed to use other toolings for asset creation and management, and when I do, I would dedicate articles to those tools as they apply to game development.

I started working with Rust a while back (Roughly a year now), my confidence in my ability to use its tooling is growing by the day, and I intend to use that as the primary language for my game development and research (I have good expertise with Python Programming, and I intend to use that for scripting when possible). In that same vein, I have decided to go with the Bevy Engine for game development in Rust.

Why Rust

Rust feels like the next logical mutation of my craft; sharp, uncompromising, and strangely elegant. When you’re trying to sculpt worlds where every microsecond can make or break the illusion, safety and performance aren’t luxuries; they’re the foundations of the universe. If I’m going to build digital worlds, I want their limits to be the boundaries of physics, not the fragility of my code..

In games, most times, a lot of things are happening at the same time, or the illusion of a lot of things happening at once is one that the game developer invokes in the minds of the players. Rust's concurrency model offers a sweet support for such a feature, allowing concurrent processing of things to optimize events.

Rust has amazing documentation and support. The Rust community is a very active, religious-like community; there is almost always someone or a reference to help clarify any issues you might be facing with your code logic or program. This understanding creates a motivating mindset and helps new developers get access to support, information, and even tooling to improve their productivity. You definitely do not want to spend days trying to resolve a programming-related issue when you could focus more on your game narrative, story, and world.

Why Bevy

And then there is Bevy, a young Rust-based game engine. I chose Bevy because of the reasons mentioned for Rust, since it is a game engine built in Rust, but it also has some independent perks that make it a choice for my journey

The thought put into Bevy is innovative and beautiful; it is a very data-centric game engine, which is the basis of any world; Data! Allowing game developers to model simple and complex game logics with a simple, systematic approach.

Bevy is also very fast, both in operation and in compile times, which becomes a big deal when making iterative changes to your games during development.

Since this article is written at the start of my journey, I can not speak on the technical sides of things. I have little to no real working experience using Bevy, but from my research, it has proven to be an excellent choice to commit to, and like the saying goes, “You can never know until you try”.

  • You can never know until you try

The Road Ahead

Since this is a hobby, I intend to have a systematic and consistent interval of work, documenting my progress in the open, and helping someone like me out there looking for a nice reference for learning game development. I am open to collaboration and corrections to the content and information I put out.

If this sort of thing resonates with you, you should consider subscribing to my articles to get an update when I drop new posts. In the meantime, I would continue to work on my hobby of game development. Until next time. Adios

entry.title: How to Implement Autocomplete Functionality for Your CLI Program in Python
entry.content:
Motivation

While taking on a coding challenge on the codecrafters platform. I was tasked to implement an autocompletion feature for my shell project. While researching how autocompletion works under the hood for most popular shell programs, I came across the readline standard Python module which provides an interface round the GNU Readline library.

The readline module defines a number of functions to facilitate completion and reading/writing of history files from the Python interpreter.

Introduction

Building a command‑line interface is a bit like conducting a conversation with a very literal friend. They wait for your every word, take everything at face value, and never finish your sentences , unless you teach them how. That’s where autocomplete comes in.

In this guide, we’ll explore how to add smooth, shell‑like tab completion to a Python CLI program. We’ll draw inspiration from the readline library, a small but mighty tool that can make your interface feel remarkably alive.

Why Autocomplete Matters

A CLI with autocomplete feels like a machine that understands your intentions or at least predicts your vocabulary. It saves keystrokes, reduces errors, and gives your program a professional, polished feeling. Anyone who’s used Bash, Zsh, or Fish knows the joy of tapping Tab and watching the program finish their thought.

We’re going to recreate a slice of that magic.

The Core Idea

Autocomplete in Python generally works through the readline library. This library lets you:

  • Capture user input with a customizable editing experience.
  • Bind keys (like Tab) to specific behaviors.
  • Install a completer function that decides what suggestions to serve.

The flow looks like this:

  1. User presses Tab.
  2. readline calls your completer function.
  3. Your function returns a possible match.
  4. readline cycles through the options as Tab is pressed repeatedly.

Simple but elegant.

A Practical Example: Building a Vocabulary-Based Completer

Below is a clean snippet that demonstrates how to create and register a simple completer that suggests words from a predefined vocabulary.

def make_completer(vocabulary):
  # https://docs.python.org/3/library/rlcompleter.html#rlcompleter.Completer
  def custom_complete(text, state):
  # None is returned for the end of the completion session.
  results = [x + " " for x in vocabulary if x.startswith(text)] + [None]
  
  # A space is added to the completion since the Python readline doesn't
  # do this on its own. When a word is fully completed we want to mimic
  # the default readline library behavior of adding a space after it.
  return results[state]
return custom_complete


vocabulary = {'echo', 'exit'}
readline.parse_and_bind("tab: complete")
readline.parse_and_bind("bind ^I rl_complete")
readline.set_completer(make_completer(vocabulary))

Let’s break down what’s happening.

Understanding the Completer Function

The make_completer() function generates a nested custom_complete() function tailored to the vocabulary you provide.

When the user types:

e

and presses Tab, custom_complete() steps in and returns options like:

echo
exit

It adds a trailing space because Python’s readline does not automatically separate completed words. This little flourish makes the experience feel more natural.

Binding the Tab Key

This part can get interesting depending on your system.

Standard GNU Readline

On many Linux systems, this line is enough:

# this would work on most linux system
readline.parse_and_bind("tab: complete")

macOS (using libedit)

macOS ships with editline, a readline impersonator with its own dialect. The line above won’t work alone, so you add:

readline.parse_and_bind("bind ^I rl_complete")

This tells libedit: “When the user presses Tab (^I), run the completer."

Together, these bindings give your CLI the behavior you expect.

Using the Completer in a CLI Loop

Once your completer is set up, you can drop it into an input loop like:

while True:
  command = input("$ ").strip()
  # process command

Now, each time your user begins a word and taps Tab, suggestions spring to life.

Extending the Concept

This basic vocabulary match is just the beginning. You can expand the idea in powerful ways:

  • Different vocabularies depending on context.
  • Directory and file completion.
  • Subcommand trees (like Git or Docker).
  • Dynamic completions from APIs or internal state.

Once you get comfortable, you can build a CLI that rivals many native tools.

Final Thoughts

Autocomplete transforms a stiff prompt into a partner in dialogue. With just a few thoughtful lines of Python, your CLI can anticipate the user’s needs, usher them gently forward, and turn typing into more of a dance than a chore.

The code above plants the seed, what grows from it is up to you.

entry.title: How to generate an ERD for your Database with Python in seconds
entry.content:
Scenic Mountain picture by TERADAT SANTIVIVUT

TL;DR

  • Install eralchemy2 (if you have an issue in this step, visit the solution at the bottom)
  • Import render_er function from eralchemy2 package
  • (Optional) Replace +asyncpg in your DB URL if you’re using async database connection.
  • Call render_er() to generate a .png. It takes two parameters: your database connection string and the string path to save the image to.
  • Admire your handiwork.

Introduction

An Entity–Relationship Diagram (ERD) is a type of data modeling diagram used to visually represent the structure of a database. It illustrates the entities (tables) within a system, their attributes (columns), and the relationships that exist between them. ERDs are commonly used during the design phase of database development to provide a high-level understanding of how data elements interact and are organized.

The concept of ERDs was first introduced by Peter Chen in 1976 as part of the Entity–Relationship model, which aimed to create a more natural and conceptual view of data. Over time, ERDs have become a standard tool in database design and are widely supported by modern database management and modeling software.

An ERD typically consists of three primary components:

  1. Entities—Represented as rectangles, entities correspond to database tables that store specific data objects (e.g., Users, Orders, Products).
  2. Attributes—Represented as ovals or listed within entities, these describe the properties of each entity (e.g., id, name, email).
  3. Relationships—Represented as lines connecting entities, these indicate how data in one table relates to data in another, often defined through primary and foreign keys.

ERDs are used by software engineers, database administrators, and data analysts to communicate the logical structure of databases, ensuring clarity, consistency, and efficient system design. They play an essential role in both conceptual and physical database modeling, bridging the gap between abstract data theory and practical implementation.

Example of ERD Diagram

A sample ERD

Why This Matters

In modern data-driven apps, your schema is a living thing; constantly evolving. An ERD keeps it visible,** understandable**, and** collaborative**.

As developers, we spend too much time spelunking through migrations and table definitions. Let’s give our eyes a break; and our diagrams some love.

Script to Generate ERD

from app.settings import Settings
from eralchemy2 import render_er

# i prefer to load my environment variables with Pydantic-setting BaseSetting Model
settings = Settings()

SYNC_DATABASE_URL = settings.DATABASE_URL.replace("+asyncpg", "")

render_er(SYNC_DATABASE_URL, 'erd_from_sqlite.png')

After running this script, an new image file will be created with the name you passed the second argument to the render_er function.

Common Tips & Pitfalls

  • Async Database URL won’t work with eralchemy2 as at the time of writing this.
  • If nothing shows up: Make sure your database is accessible and populated with actual tables.
  • SQLite quirks: If you’re using SQLite in-memory (sqlite:///:memory:), it won’t persist for introspection. Use a file-based or external DB instead.
  • Make it part of CI: Automate ERD generation so your team always has an up-to-date schema map.

Common Issue with Installing Graphviz on macOS
Sometimes when installing, there is an issue with the installation.

Solution

export C_INCLUDE_PATH="$(brew --prefix graphviz)/include/"
export LIBRARY_PATH="$(brew --prefix graphviz)/lib/"
pip install --use-pep517 --config-setting="--global-option=build_ext" pygraphviz

Final Thought

With just a few lines of Python, you can turn your database schema into a visual map; a living portrait of your data’s architecture. A simple tool, a tiny script, but then the structure of your data model can be communicated more visually.

entry.title: Zed: The Text Editor Reimagined for the Modern Developer
entry.content:
Why Zed might just change the way you write software.

Guide to Setup and Configure Zed Editor

Why switching to Zed might improve your workflow as a developer.

As a developer, the text editor is the one software application you would spend most of your time crafting programs, scripts, and updating text related to software development. It is only reasonable that you get the most out of your primary text editor of choice.

Why Zed!

  • It’s New, Modern, and Built for the Future: Zed isn’t just another text editor; it’s a re-imagination of what a coding environment should feel like in the age of blazing-fast CPUs, cloud collaboration, and intelligent code assistance. Born from the creators of Atom (Atom was my first ever experience with text editors when I started programming).
  • It’s Very Fast : Speed isn’t just a bragging right; it’s a philosophy. Zed is implemented in Rust, a language celebrated for its performance and safety. That means no Electron bloat, no sluggish startup, and no “fans going supersonic” moments. Opening large projects feels effortless. Searching across thousands of files happens in a blink. The editor responds to your typing as if it’s reading your mind; not your CPU cycles. Zed makes “instant” feel normal again.
  • It’s Open Source and Transparent: Zed’s source code is fully open on GitHub; transparent, hackable, and alive with community input. You can explore the internals, submit improvements, or simply watch the evolution of one of the most ambitious open-source editors in recent years. Unlike many modern tools that hide their logic behind corporate curtains. This is particularly interesting if you’re a Rust developer, since the Zed extension ecosystem is still young, you can write your own extension that would become the foundation for developers in a few years.
  • It’s Written in Rust; for Developers, by Developers: By writing Zed entirely in Rust, the team didn’t just chase performance, they embraced correctness and safety. This foundation gives developers confidence that the tool they rely on most won’t buckle under pressure. Rust’s concurrency model also allows Zed to manage multiple tasks at once, background indexing, syntax parsing, and collaborative sessions, without skipping a beat. It’s not just fast; it’s predictably fast
  • It’s Simple, Beautiful, and Purposeful: Zed’s interface is an ode to minimalism. It’s clean, distraction-free, and elegant without being sterile. No cluttered panes or noisy toolbars fighting for your attention. Every pixel has intent. Whether you’re working in a dark room late into the night or in a bright café, Zed’s design feels at home. The UI becomes an extension of your mind, just you and your code, nothig else.
  • It’s AI-centric, integrates upcoming LLMs into your workflow to generate, transform, and analyze code. Where most editors treat AI as a plugin or novelty, Zed is building it into the heart of the workflow. It’s designed to integrate seamlessly with large language models (LLMs) to work with codes without breaking your flow.
  • it’s Built for Collaboration: When I first experienced the add contact feature in Zed, I was wowed, it felt more like a social media for developers, and that gave me more reasons to adore the intentionality put into the development of the text editor.

If any of these attributes interest you just a little bit, just wait and see the comparison against a popular option.

How does Zed compare against VSCode?

FeatureVSCodeZed
Startup time⚡ Slow (Electron)⚡⚡ Instant (Rust native)
Memory useHeavyLight
CollaborationExtensions requiredBuilt-in multiplayer
AI toolsCopilotNative integration planned
UI/UXCustomizable but denseMinimal and elegant
LicenseMITOpen Source
EcosystemMaturedYoung

Installation

If you do not already have Zed installed on your computer, follow this link to the Zed official page to download the version for your operating system. Currently, Zed supports macOS, Windows, and Linux.

After download and installation, you can proceed to start a new instance of the Zed Editor on your computer.

If you’re like me, coming from a VSCode background, you must understand the great ergonomics gotten from interacting with VSCode from the terminal and vice versa. This can be your reality too; in order to gain this ability, you would need to install the Zed CLI. An example of the benefits gained from installing the CLI is opening a directory from the terminal in Zed with a command like zed ..

Install Zed CLI

On Linux, the Zed CLI should come with the Linux distribution’s Zed package, as seen from the download step above. On macOS, the CLI comes with the binary and can be installed into your system via the command palette.

I would focus on macOS for this guide, since I am using a Mac.

You can access Zed’s Command Palette, which is very similar to the command palette found in VSCode. You can open the command palette with the following key binding: cmd + shift + p

Searching the command palette for cli: install would show the command for installing the CLI.

Choosing a Theme Extension

The minimalistic interface of the Zed editor can be greatly improved by choosing a theme that best aligns with your personality and self. For me, coming from VSCode and having worked with a certain shade of theme for a while, my go-to theme is this.

Steps to install a theme extension

  • Open Command Palette with cmd + shift + p
  • Select zed: extension
  • Select Theme Tab
  • Search for the Theme of your choice and install

Once you’ve installed a theme of your choosing, you can toggle between these themes using the theme selector: toggle command in the command palette.

I use Colorizer for my local development, because it offers a vibrant color contrast look and feel to text.

Screenshot showing the Colorizer theme

Command Keys Bindings

  • cmd + shift + p: opens the command palette for the text editor.
  • cmd + j: Toggles the integrated terminal within the editor.
  • cmd + b: Toggles the sidebar visibility.
  • cmd + k + 0: Collapse all regions in the current active text file (code region refers to function bodies and block structures)
  • cmd + k + j: Expand all regions in the current text editor. This is the opposite of the command above.
  • cmd + p: Finds a file in the current working directory.
  • cmd + k + w: Close all open tabs in the editor
  • cmd + shift + f: Search all files in the current directory for text match

Conclusion

Zed is still relatively new compared to matured editors like VSCode, so it’s still lacking some features that you might have seen in other text editors, regardless, for what it does have, it does them very. It was built with the pain point of modern developers in mind, it’s embraced AI to boost development rate and keeps the developer flow at all time high with little to no noise from the UI. I am still very new to Zed, But I do intend to make it my new best editor moving forward.

entry.title: 6 Python Tips That Quietly Level Up Your Code
entry.content:
Introduction

If you're like me at the moment, you've gotten to a point in your software development journey where you find yourself writing code to tick off tasks from a task board or complete features for a sprint. At such times, the focus sometimes shifts from poetic code to functional code (not implying that functional code cannot be easily poetic, but it takes mastery and experience to maintain such quality when working under tight deadlines). It is at this point that you're more concerned with getting things to work than with how they feel and look.

Below are some Python tips and tricks I use and believe are not as emphasized as they should be. They would do good to your mental health when writing code and, more importantly, when updating that code 3 months from now.

TL;DR:

  1. Inline single-line blocks in block expressions
  2. Use underscores to delimit a large number
  3. Dictionary comprehension
  4. Using the setdefault dictionary method
  5. Ignore exceptions with contextlib.suppress
  6. Multiple statements on a single line

1. Inline single-line blocks in block expressions

some_condition = True

if some_condition:
    print("Some Condition is True")
else:
    print("Some Condition is Falsey")

In the code sample above, the correct conventional 4-space indentation is used for the expression in a block expression. But in this particular case, the block contains just a single expression. This might be a trivial case, but many such scenarios arise a lot in functional codebases, and you can save some real estate by inlining the single expression on the same line as the if block.

some_condition = True

if some_condition: print("Some Condition is True")
else: print("Some Condition is False")

This is perfectly valid Python, and in some cases makes your code easier to read and follow. Do note that you can only inline single-line expressions; if the expression is multi-line, you have to use the conventional 4-space indentation to communicate the block scope to the Python interpreter. If, however, always using the block format for block expressions works better for you, by all means do use that way.

2. Use underscores to delimit a large number

This is more common than some of the tips on this list. Still, for the uninitiated, here goes nothing. When dealing with literal values in your application, it can be counterintuitive or even error-prone having to figure out the value of a large literal number at a glance, and this could very well mean the only thing standing between you and your continued state of mental flow. Python — and some other high-level programming languages like Rust — allows the use of _ in literal numbers to show their unit.

obscure_large_number = 3422345365
clear_large_number = 3_422_345_365  # it is easier to tell the unit value when delimited by underscores

3. Dictionary comprehension

The more popular sibling of the comprehension family in Python is the list comprehension, where a list is generated from an iterable in a single expression without needing a conventional for-loop to populate the list. This same process can be used to generate a dictionary or a set.

Let's imagine we have a list of names and want to generate a dictionary whose key is a name and whose value is the length of that name's characters. We can achieve this with a traditional for-loop, like so:

names = ["Brian", "Anthony", "Maryann", "Joseph", "Emediong"]
word_count = {}
for name in names:
    word_count[name] = len(name)

print(word_count)

# Output
# {'Brian': 5, 'Anthony': 7, 'Maryann': 7, 'Joseph': 6, 'Emediong': 8}

Now this same functionality can be achieved through dictionary comprehension in a more comprehensive way (pun intended). It looks just like a list comprehension, but curly braces are used, and a colon separates the key from the value being derived from the iterable.

names = ["Brian", "Anthony", "Maryann", "Joseph", "Emediong"]
word_count = {name: len(name) for name in names}

# general dictionary comprehension syntax
# {key: derived_value for key in sequence}

print(word_count)

# Output
# {'Brian': 5, 'Anthony': 7, 'Maryann': 7, 'Joseph': 6, 'Emediong': 8}

4. Using the setdefault dictionary method

Still on the topic of working with dictionaries in Python: there are times you wish to update a value in a dictionary, but you have to ensure that said key already exists in the dictionary, or Python would raise a KeyError. You could write a one-liner to check for the existence of the key before updating the key's value, like so:

race_laps = {"Brian": 234, "Anthony": 525, "Maryann": 534, "Joseph": 467, "Emediong": 876}


new_lap_data = {
    "Brian": 34,
    "Anthony": 45,
    "Felix": 100,
}

for driver, distance in new_lap_data.items():
    if driver in race_laps:
        race_laps[driver] += distance
    else:
        race_laps[driver] = distance

But it is clear that this introduces unnecessary verbosity into our program by introducing an if/else block. We can use the setdefault method of a dictionary to set a default value for a key before trying to update it, in case it is not present in the dictionary. The same logic above can be rewritten like so with the setdefault method:

race_laps = {"Brian": 234, "Anthony": 525, "Maryann": 534, "Joseph": 467, "Emediong": 876}

new_lap_data = {
    "Brian": 34,
    "Anthony": 45,
    "Felix": 100,
}

for driver, distance in new_lap_data.items():
    race_laps.setdefault(driver, 0)  # this sets a value of 0 for the driver if not already in the dictionary
    race_laps[driver] += distance

This approach makes the code more concise and is more Pythonic than the structure with the if/else block.

5. Ignore exceptions with contextlib.suppress

Sometimes we want to catch an exception and then do nothing with it — we're catching it to prevent the program from breaking or stopping, and to continue with the flow. This can be done with a try/except block, and if you have no logic to run in the except block, you can use the pass statement to indicate nothingness.

def do_some_action():
    # some action that might fail but is not critical to the whole program
    pass

while True:
    try:
        do_some_action()
    except Exception:
        pass

In the code sample above, we put the logic that might raise an exception in the try block and then ignore the cases where it raises. This structure forces us to use a block; we could apply the first tip from this post to further improve the structure and gain some real estate.

def do_some_action():
    # some action that might fail but is not critical to the whole program
    pass

while True:
    try: do_some_action()
    except Exception: pass

However, we can go even further and use a standard library class that is not very well known, to suppress exceptions and continue with your program as if they hadn't happened. The contextlib standard library provides a class called suppress that can be used to suppress exceptions in our code. Going back to the same example as above, the code can be rewritten with suppress as follows:

from contextlib import suppress


def do_some_action():
    # some action that might fail but is not critical to the whole program
    pass

while True:
    with suppress(Exception):  # the exception is suppressed silently
        do_some_action()

This suppresses the exception type passed to it, and just like the normal exception rule, a parent class can suppress child exception classes. You can also suppress multiple exceptions with a with block by passing more exception classes to suppress, separated by commas.

with suppress(ValueError, ValidationError):  # ValueError and ValidationError are suppressed here
    ...

6. Multiple statements on a single line

Conventionally, a newline in Python code declares the end of a statement and the start of another. Some other programming languages use semicolons to separate statements, but Python is a whitespace language. Regardless, semicolons can be used in Python, and in rare situations you might need to put more than one statement on a single line — you can do this by terminating each statement with a semicolon.

# Conventional Python statement flow
# each newline denotes a different statement
a = 1
b = 2
print(f"A = {a}")
print(f"B = {b}")

# using semicolons to separate statements
a = 1;  # this is also valid Python
b = 3;
print(f"A = {a}");

# putting multiple statements on a single line
a = 10;print(f"A = {a}")

Clearly, putting each statement on its own line leads to better readability for your code, but in rare scenarios, knowing that multiple statements can be placed on a single line can give you the ability to do certain magic.

Conclusion

I love reading and learning about these little neat tricks and try to apply them when I see fit in my projects. If there are similar tricks you know and would love to share, I'd love to hear them.

entry.title: My FastAPI Project Blueprint
entry.content:
I've refined this structure in production environments serving over 500+ concurrent users; it scales effortlessly, stays sane to maintain, and keeps productivity at full throttle.

TL;DR

If you just want to use the template FastAPI structure directly in your project, check out this GitHub repo for the complete project structure.

Introduction

I have worked with FastAPI almost daily in the last year. During that period, I developed a standard project structure that works exceptionally well to keep me motivated to make changes and add features easily, and it also scales incredibly.

In this post, I will break down every part of my FastAPI go-to architecture — the one I optimize whenever I'm starting a new project or refactoring an old one. Whether you're trying to ship ideas faster, organize your growing codebase, or harden your app's security, this structure will help you build confidently and evolve your project like a pro.

Project Structure

.
├── Makefile
├── logs/
│   └── app.log
└── app/
    ├── __init__.py
    ├── api_router.py
    ├── dependencies.py
    ├── logger.py
    ├── main.py
    ├── middlewares.py
    ├── settings.py
    ├── routers/
    │   ├── admin.py
    │   ├── auth.py
    │   └── products.py
    ├── schemas/
    │   ├── admin.py
    │   ├── auth.py
    │   └── products.py
    └── services/
        ├── admin.py
        ├── auth.py
        └── products.py

The App Directory

The app directory is the engine and core of the application. It contains all the modules and code needed to power the majority of use cases for a backend infrastructure. I'll explain each directory and module in the app directory and justify their use, pointing out common issues and highlighting steps taken to improve code quality and developer experience.

__init__.py

It is standard practice to include an __init__.py file in every Python package; this helps to declare a folder as a regular Python package.

api_router.py

I use this as a central module for managing all my routers in my application. This enables me to have features like version controlling with /v1/users, /v2/users while keeping the codebase easy to follow and clean.

# app/api_router.py

from fastapi import APIRouter

api_v1 = APIRouter(prefix="/v1")
api_v2 = APIRouter(prefix="/v2")

# include routes to a root route
# from app.routers import routers as user_routers
# api_v1.include_router(users_routers)

logger.py

Logging is a crucial part of every software application. It gives visibility into the operation of any running software application and can help guide resolution of issues and bugs when they do happen — and they will happen.

Instead of getting overwhelmed with configurations, this template works for me in almost all my projects. You can extend it by setting up an external handler to connect your log records to a pretty dashboard or analytics tool. This particular configuration allows me to group logs by day, achieved with the TimedRotatingFileHandler, making the process of debugging much easier.

# app/logger.py

import logging
import json

from logging.handlers import TimedRotatingFileHandler

logger = logging.getLogger()


class JsonFormatter(logging.Formatter):
    def format(self, record):
        log_record = {
            "timestamp": self.formatTime(record, self.datefmt),
            "level": record.levelname,
            "module": record.module,
            "funcName": record.funcName,
            "lineno": record.lineno,
            "message": record.getMessage(),
        }
        return json.dumps(log_record)


file_handler = TimedRotatingFileHandler(
    "logs/app.log", when="midnight", interval=1 / 86400, backupCount=7
)

file_handler.setFormatter(JsonFormatter())

logger.handlers = [file_handler]
logger.setLevel(logging.INFO)

main.py

The main module is the entry point into the application. Most of the security policies and rules for the application are set up here.

# app/main.py

from contextlib import asynccontextmanager
from datetime import datetime, UTC
from fastapi import FastAPI

from starlette.middleware.trustedhost import TrustedHostMiddleware
from starlette.middleware.base import BaseHTTPMiddleware
from fastapi.middleware.gzip import GZipMiddleware
from fastapi.middleware.cors import CORSMiddleware
from fastapi.responses import RedirectResponse
from fastapi.responses import JSONResponse
from fastapi.requests import Request
from fastapi import HTTPException
from fastapi import FastAPI

from slowapi import Limiter
from slowapi.util import get_remote_address

from redis import asyncio as aioredis

from app.logger import logger
from app.api_router import api
from app.settings import Settings
from app.middlewares import log_request_middleware

settings = Settings()


@asynccontextmanager
async def lifespan(app: FastAPI):
    yield


def initiate_app():
    app = FastAPI(
        title="FastAPI Sample Project",
        summary="API for FastAPI Sample Project",
        lifespan=lifespan,
    )

    origins = [
        # Add allowed origins here
    ]

    app.add_middleware(
        CORSMiddleware,
        allow_origins=origins,
        allow_credentials=True,
        allow_methods=["*"],
        allow_headers=["*"],
    )

    # tweak this to see the most efficient size
    app.add_middleware(GZipMiddleware, minimum_size=100)
    app.add_middleware(
        TrustedHostMiddleware,
        allowed_hosts=[
            # Add allowed hosts here, this controls host that the application can be hosted on
        ],
    )
    app.add_middleware(BaseHTTPMiddleware, dispatch=log_request_middleware)

    # this handles rate limiting protecting the API from abuse or Denial of Service Attacks
    limiter = Limiter(key_func=get_remote_address)
    app.state.limiter = limiter

    app.include_router(api)
    return app


app = initiate_app()


@app.exception_handler(HTTPException)
async def http_exception_handler(request: Request, exc: HTTPException):
    return JSONResponse(
        status_code=exc.status_code,
        content={
            "detail": exc.detail,
            "path": request.url.path,
            "timestamp": datetime.now(UTC).isoformat(),
        },
    )


@app.exception_handler(Exception)
async def global_exception_handler(request: Request, exc: Exception):
    logger.error(f"Unexpected error: {str(exc)}")

    return JSONResponse(
        status_code=500,
        content={
            "detail": "An unexpected error occurred",
            "path": request.url.path,
        },
    )


@app.get("/", tags=["Root"])
async def root():
    # this redirects root requests to the docs page
    return RedirectResponse("/docs")

settings.py

I have discovered that using Pydantic's BaseSettings model makes handling of environment variables easy and clean. Types can be defined for the environment variables and they are validated at app startup time, and default values can be provided for optional environment variables.

# app/settings.py

from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings
from pydantic import ConfigDict, AnyUrl


class Settings(BaseSettings):
    model_config = ConfigDict(env_file=".env")

    example_secret: str = "example secret value"

    JWT_SECRET: str  # required environment variable
    JWT_ALGORITHM: str = "HS256"  # optional environment variable with default value

dependencies.py

I use this module to group my custom route dependencies. Common dependencies like get_db, which is commonly used to get a session to interact with the database, can be declared here. Using a dedicated module for dependencies makes code organization better and more modular, since usually different routes depend on these dependencies. Testing is also easier since logic can be tested in isolation.

middlewares.py

I use this module to group all the custom middlewares I define for my application. The modular benefits outlined for a dedicated dependencies module also apply here.

Directories

Routers

I find that creating a module for each logical grouping of routes makes development lovely and easier — for example, an auth.py module for all routes relating to user authentication and profile management, a products.py module for all routes relating to product management, and admin.py for all routes related to the admin API.

I try to keep my route functions to at most 2 lines of code. The route function simply lays out the route and defines the dependencies and query parameters needed, while the logic for each route function is defined in a service function.

# app/routers/auth.py

from typing import Annotated

from pydantic import EmailStr
from fastapi.routing import APIRouter
from sqlalchemy.ext.asyncio import AsyncSession
from fastapi import Depends, Body, BackgroundTasks

from app.dependencies import get_db
from app.schemas import auth as auth_schemas
from app.services import auth as auth_services

router = APIRouter(prefix="/auth", tags=["Authentication"])


EmailBody = Annotated[EmailStr, Body(embed=True)]
DBDep = Annotated[AsyncSession, Depends(get_db)]


@router.post("/signup", response_model=auth_schemas.UserModel)
async def signup(
    db: DBDep,
    bg_task: BackgroundTasks,
    request_data: auth_schemas.UserSignUpData,
):
    return await auth_services.signup_user(request_data, db, bg_task)

The route function is easy on the eyes: the business logic is handled in the service function, while the route focuses on defining the dependencies and requirements in the form of a JSON body or query parameters.

Schemas

All my Pydantic models go into the schema module. Just like the routers directory, the schemas directory houses all the schema modules. Usually I match each route module with a corresponding schema module and a service module — this way each component of my application is grouped in a very logical and predictable way. An example of a schema module is auth.py, shown below.

# app/schemas/auth.py

from uuid import UUID
from datetime import datetime
from typing import Annotated

from pydantic import BaseModel, EmailStr, Field


class UserSignUpData(BaseModel):
    password: Annotated[str, Field(min_length=8)]
    email: Annotated[EmailStr, Field(max_length=254)]


class UserModel(BaseModel):
    id: UUID

    email: EmailStr
    date_created: datetime
    date_updated: datetime

Services

The services directory houses modules with the actual business logic to process the backend functionality. This can include API calls to third-party services, functions to make query calls to the database, and so on. Separating them this way allows a major separation of concerns between the route's API requirements and the actual implementation.

And just like I do for the routers and schemas directories, I match each module in those directories with a corresponding module for the component covered in the services directory. Working with the running example for the auth component:

# app/services/auth.py

from datetime import timedelta

from fastapi import HTTPException
from passlib.context import CryptContext
from fastapi.security import OAuth2PasswordBearer

from sqlalchemy import select
from sqlalchemy.ext.asyncio import AsyncSession

from app.settings import Settings
from app.models import User as UserDB
from app.schemas import auth as auth_schema

settings = Settings()

JWT_SECRET = settings.JWT_SECRET
JWT_ALGORITHM = settings.JWT_ALGORITHM

ACCESS_TOKEN_LIFESPAN = timedelta(days=2)
REFRESH_TOKEN_LIFESPAN = timedelta(days=5)

pwd_context = CryptContext(schemes=["bcrypt"], deprecated="auto")
oauth2_scheme = OAuth2PasswordBearer(tokenUrl="v1/auth/token")


def verify_password(plain_password: str, hashed_password: str):
    return pwd_context.verify(plain_password, hashed_password)


def get_password_hash(password: str):
    return pwd_context.hash(password)


async def get_user(email: str, session: AsyncSession) -> UserDB | None:
    stmt = select(UserDB).where(UserDB.email == email)
    result = await session.execute(stmt)
    return result.scalar_one_or_none()


async def create_user(
    user_data: auth_schema.UserSignUpData,
    session: AsyncSession,
):
    result = await session.execute(
        select(UserDB).where(UserDB.email == user_data.email)
    )
    if result.scalar_one_or_none():
        raise HTTPException(status_code=400, detail="Email already registered")

    result = await session.execute(
        select(UserDB).where(UserDB.email == user_data.email)
    )
    if result.scalar_one_or_none():
        raise HTTPException(status_code=400, detail="Username already used")

    hashed_password = get_password_hash(user_data.password)
    new_user = UserDB(
        email=user_data.email,
        password=hashed_password,
        username=user_data.email,
    )

    session.add(new_user)
    await session.commit()
    await session.refresh(new_user)
    return new_user


async def signup_user(
    data: auth_schema.UserSignUpData,
    session: AsyncSession,
):
    return await create_user(data, session)

The Makefile

Outside the core backend Python concerns, I have come to appreciate making use of tools like make to simplify invocation of common command line tools — like starting a FastAPI server, starting a pytest session, and so on.

# Makefile

run-local:
	fastapi dev app/main.py

test-local:
	pytest -s --cov

coverage-report:
	coverage report

coverage-html:
	coverage report && coverage html

In order to use the make tool you have to have make installed on your computer.

With this file in place at the root of my project, whenever I want to start my FastAPI server, I can do so with the following command:

make run-local

Instead of typing out the full command. This contributes to increased productivity when running certain command line tools over and over again.

Conclusion

I ignored setup for database connections in this template.

Maintaining a modular project structure and codebase does more for you down the line than you might think. A predictable and reasonable organization of functionality and tools gives beauty to a codebase beyond the functionality itself.

Inasmuch as this pattern has improved my productivity in the past year, I actively seek to learn and adopt better and better approaches to constructing and crafting my backend infrastructure.

entry.title: How I Hacked FastAPI BackgroundTasks for Real-Time Progress Updates (Without Celery)
entry.content:
I Built a FastAPI Endpoint That Runs in the Background and Talks Back

Image was generated with ChatGPT

I Built a FastAPI Endpoint That Runs in the Background and Talks Back

Intro

Recently, at work, I had to build a set of REST API endpoints to trigger an AI model process that could take several minutes to complete. The usual options weren’t ideal:

  • Long-polling from the frontend until the result is ready (wasteful).
  • Blocking the request until the model finishes (terrible UX).
  • Fire-and-forget background job with an email notification at the end (better, but not interactive).

Clearly, running the process in the background is efficient since it frees up the application to handle other requests. But here’s the problem: I wanted to peek into the current state of the background process and report progress back to the client—without committing to a heavyweight background manager like Celery.

Problem

You kick off an AI model through a FastAPI endpoint. It takes minutes. Your frontend can either keep hammering with polls, freeze the request until it’s done, or dump the job into a background worker and email the result later.

None of those felt right for me. I wanted real-time progress updates—without bringing in Celery, Redis, or Kubernetes-sized machinery. So I hacked FastAPI’s BackgroundTasks into whispering back status updates while it ran. Here’s how.

FastAPI supports background tasks through the BackgroundTasks dependency. But it’s fire-and-forget. Once a task starts, you get no insight into its progress or result in real-time. Need to peek behind the curtain? You're out of luck—unless you add some extra plumbing.

Solution

FastApi comes with a BackgroundTasks for managing Background tasks in a route, but it posses no native way of interacting with those background task once they have been initiated.

below is a simple example of a route that initiates a background task that prints the numbers to a million

# main.py
import time
from fastapi import FastAPI, BackgroundTasks

app = FastAPI()

def count_to(n: int, job_id: str, update_progress: Callable[..., Awaitable[None]]) -> int:
    """
    Iterates from 1 up to n and returns the values of n
    This is meant to be used to represent a slow running function.
    """
    result = 1
    for i in range(1, n):
        update_progress(job_id, "processing", round((i / n) * 100, 2))
        print(f"{i}")
        result = i

    update_progress(job_id, "completed", 100, result, ended_at=time.time())
    return result

@app.post("/tasks")
async def initiate_task(background_task: BackgroundTasks):
    background_task.add_task(count_to)
    return {"detail": "Task Started Successfully"}

You can run the FastAPI application with the followings commands

fastapi dev main.py

if you visit the endpoint you would immediately get a response that says

curl localhost:8000/tasks -X POST

# {"detail":"Task Started Successfully"}%

And if you look at your application logs, you would see that numbers were printed from 1 through 999999

This shows that the route started the count_to function in the background and immediately returned a message to the client

Now, There is no direct way to obtain information about the running background task and report to the client (this can be setup with Redis and other Background process tools but for a simple case like us).

I achieved this by making a global data structure to keep track of all the background task so that at any point after the background task has been started I can refer to this data structure to get update about the current state of the task and possibly it result

import uuid 
import time
from typing import Callable, Awaitable

from fastapi import FastAPI, BackgroundTasks, HTTPException


app = FastAPI()

task_jobs = {}


def count_to(n: int, job_id: str, update_progress: Callable[..., int]) -> int:
    """
    Iterates from 1 up to n and returns the values of n
    This is meant to be used to represent a slow running function.
    """
    result = 1
    for i in range(1, n):
        update_progress(job_id, "processing", round((i / n) * 100, 2))
        print(f"{i}")
        result = i

    update_progress(job_id, "completed", 100, result, ended_at=time.time())
    return result


@app.post("/tasks")
async def initiate_task(background_task: BackgroundTasks):
    job_id = str(uuid.uuid4())

    # register the task to the task db
    task_jobs[job_id] = {
        "status": "initiated",
        "progress": 0.0,
        "result": None,
        "errors": None,
    }

    def update_task(job_id: str, status: str, progress: float | int, result = None, errors = None):
        if not job_id in task_jobs:
            return
        
        task_jobs.update({
          "status": status,
          "progress": progress,
        })

        if result:
            task_jobs[job_id]["result"] = result
        if errors:
            task_jobs[job_id]["errors"] = errors

    background_task.add_task(count_to, 1_000_000, job_id, update_task)
    return {"message": "task started", "job_id": job_id}


@app.get("/tasks/status")
async def get_task_status(job_id: str):
    if not job_id in task_jobs:
        raise HTTPException(404, detail="Job ID not found")
    
    return task_jobs[job_id]

Demo: Checking Task Status

Trigger a job:

curl -X POST localhost:8000/tasks
# {"message":"task started", "job_id":"c32cfe25-7b9c-4e87-83ec-80e7d6dcbf9e"}

Now check its progress:

curl "localhost:8000/tasks/status?job_id=c32cfe25-7b9c-4e87-83ec-80e7d6dcbf9e"

Sample response:

{
  "status": "processing",
  "progress": 42.7,
  "result": null,
  "errors": null,
  "ended_at": null
}

When it finishes:

{
  "status": "completed",
  "progress": 100,
  "result": 999999,
  "errors": null,
  "ended_at": 1727783087.12345
}

Now your background task is no longer mute—it talks back through the global dictionary.

The route called initiate_task is a post route, that generate a unique id on each call to be able to track each task individually, the default task structure is registered in the task database (dict in our case), an inner function is defined within the route, this is important because this function would be passed into the background task as an argument to the function (task) we are tying to process in the background, now it is up to you to call the update_progress functions at different points in your background task function to update the progress of the function execution, This way, the background functions talks back through the global data structure (dict)on it current state.

“That’s it. Your FastAPI now moonlights as a background worker. Tell your boss you just saved $10K in server costs—or buy yourself snacks. You earned it.”

Potential Issues

⚠️ Heads up: BackgroundTasks.add_task expects a sync function. If you pass it an async def, it won’t be awaited properly, which means FastAPI will just launch it and hope for the best. If you need async, consider using a task queue like Celery, RQ, or a custom loop via asyncio.create_task (outside of BackgroundTasks).

And just like that, your humble FastAPI app can now juggle tasks in the background and whisper back progress updates like a responsible magician. You didn’t need Celery. You didn’t need Redis. You just needed a dict, a UUID, and a stubborn refusal to give up.

💡 Pro tip: Don’t forget to eventually replace that dict with Redis or some other reliable data store, or something else persistent, if you go to production. RAM amnesia is real.
